To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the 2008 global recession caused a significant decrease (1–2 pptv) in surface ozone levels over the eastern United State and a slight increase (1–2 pptv) over the Rocky Mountains, and the air quality benefits during this recession could be quickly offset in the post-recession period.
the 2008 recession led to significant decreases in nitrogen oxides emissions and surface ozone concentrations over the eastern United states and slight increases over the western United States.

(1) the 2008 recession led to significant decreases in nitrogen oxide emissions, (2) this decrease in emissions caused a 1-2 ppbv decrease in ozone concentrations over the eastern United states, (3) this decrease in ozone concentrations could be quickly offset in the post‐recessions period by the much slower rate of emissions reductions, and (4) the recession effect is most pronounced over the eastern United Sates, and is mixed in the western U.S.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of economic recession on the air quality in the United States.
how economic recession can affect air pollution, and how air pollution may affect economic recession.
the impact of the economic recession on air quality and the implications for the future of air pollution control.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the 2008 recession has had a small impact on air quality over most of the United States.
the 2008 global recession had a modest but detectable effect on air quality over much of the United States, and that this effect was largely reversible.
the recession caused an overall decrease in surface Ozone levels over the eastern US.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the recession caused an overall improvement in air quality over the eastern United State, but the gain in air quality benefit was not large enough to justify the economic cost of the recession.
the recession had a significant impact on air quality in the U.S., but the effect is temporary.
the recession caused significant changes in NOx emission, which in turn led to changes in O3 concentrations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the impact of the NOx emission reduction on surface O3 concentration is highly dependent on emission changes, which in turn are highly dependent on the economy.
the economic recession has a significant impact on air quality, and the air quality benefit from the recession could be quickly offset if the post‐recessed emission reduction rate is not accelerated.
the economic recession can have a significant impact on O3 levels, and the impact is not limited to the region of recession.
